I spent 6 years getting my PhD. Now I’m fighting for jobs that require "2 years experience, diploma preferred." 🎓🚫

The "frozen" labor market isn't just a US headline. It’s the quiet panic in our MRT carriages. 

It’s the NUS/NTU grad sending out 100 applications into a black hole. It’s the realization that our "study hard, get a good job" contract is broken.

I recently spoke to a hiring manager in Raffles Place. 

Her truth? 

"I don't need a researcher. I need someone who can use AI to do the work of three people by Tuesday."

The market doesn't pay for your potential anymore. It pays for your utility.

We are facing a "White Collar Recession" where prestige is a liability and adaptability is the only currency. 

The question isn't "How do I find a job?" It's "How do I become un-fireable in a frozen economy?"

Here is the "Kampung Hustle" Approach I’m using to survive:
1. The "Skills-Based" CV Rewrite
Stop listing thesis topics. Start listing P&L impact.
Translate "Research Assistant" to "Project Lead who saved 20 hours/week via automation."
2. The "Coffee Shop" Network
LinkedIn Easy Apply is a lottery. Kopi with an ex-colleague is a strategy.
Target 3 "weak ties" a week. Ask for advice, not a job.
3. The "Barbell" Income
One foot in stability (contract work), one foot in high-upside (consulting/side hustle).

Don't wait for the perfect role. Create your own revenue.
Pedigree  Specialist: Be the Swiss Army knife, not the scalpel.
Speed > Perfection: Done is better than perfect in a crisis.

"饥者易为食，渴者易为饮" 
(The hungry will eat anything; the thirsty will drink anything).

Don't be so desperate you take anything. 
Be so valuable they give you everything.

Fellow graduates, are you pivoting or holding out for the "perfect" role?🤔

Ever tried explaining Enterprise AI architecture without losing your audience in jargon?

Here's how the SAP Knowledge Graph works, explained with a Biryani restaurant! 🍛🤖👇

🍽️ 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺: 𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗟𝗟𝗠𝘀 𝗔𝗹𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗔𝗿𝗲𝗻'𝘁 𝗘𝗻𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵
Imagine hiring an eager new waiter who speaks fluent English and has read every cookbook in the world (the LLM).

A customer orders:
"Bhai, one special Dum Biryani, double leg piece, spicy brinjal gravy, raita with less curd, and a cold drink!"

Without grounding, he walks into a pantry of 5,000 unlabelled jars (raw tables like MARA, VBAK, EKPO), guesses blindly (hallucination), and brings out... Chilli Chicken with Chapati! 🤦‍♂️

LLMs bring fluency, but without grounding they lack enterprise truth, business rules, and context.

🌐 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗠𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗖𝗵𝗲𝗳'𝘀 𝗕𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻
The SAP Knowledge Graph is the semantic layer: a mind-map connecting meaning, ontology, and business context across S/4HANA, SuccessFactors, Ariba, and Signavio via semantic triples (Subject → Relationship → Object).

🤖 AI Waiter → SAP Joule (conversational interface)
🗺️ Recipe Mind-Map → Knowledge Graph (triples, rules, relationships)
🎫 Ticket Printer → Agent Harness (intent → OData/REST calls)
🍲 Degchis on Dum → S/4HANA & core apps (execution + RBAC)
📊 Accounts Ledger → SAP Datasphere (analytics & Data Products)

📦 𝗜𝗻 𝗣𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗲: 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁

Why you can't find job for 6 months? 
And why a gasoline deal can be a good thing for your career.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗶𝗻  ⛓️ 

Costs rise. Brent is around $114 a barrel, roughly 70–87% above a year ago, and US diesel is  $6+ a gallon, a record. Freight and production run on diesel, so goods get more expensive before they reach a shelf. This caused US inflation to rise to 3.7% in September. The Fed sees it and holds at 3.75–4.00% and may raise again in December. 

Companies see thinner margins, expensive credit and unpredictable demand. The first reaction is a hiring freeze. Not layoffs, just "we're not hiring".

Venture funds cannot show returns to their investors, so they push portfolio companies: cut costs or there is no next round. Public companies hear the same from analysts on earnings calls. Then comparison kicks in. If a competitor cut staff and you did not, your investors ask why. Layoffs become normal because everyone does them, not because each one is rational.

The pressure moves down the chain. A client tells its vendor "we have less to spend". The vendor has fixed costs and cannot just lower the price, so it cuts its team. An outsourced studio loses a contract and its developers and designers enter the market.

The market is also expectations. When everyone knows people are searching, interviews stretch, offers shrink or even freeze, and employed people start looking "just in case". That adds supply, which lengthens searches, which adds more anxiety.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗽𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗳𝗲𝗲𝗹 𝗶𝘁 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲  🚂 

When growth stalls, companies stop investing in measuring growth. It may sound paradoxical, but during a crisis, analytics is the first thing to be cut—because it doesn’t generate revenue directly; instead, it provides insight, and in a state of panic, insight can seem like a luxury.

Titles blur. Analyst, analytics engineer, data engineer and data scientist advertise overlapping but different jobs, so one search spreads across mismatched postings. Every hiring manager now has to justify a seat against "can tooling and AI cover part of this?"

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝗻𝘀  🤔 

 💡 If you're searching, fix what you control: show one business impact from your data work

 💡 If you are hiring, remember the pool in front of you is larger than usual, and the person across the table is probably tired

Mind the small print

A global electric behemoth has one cybersecurity policy and a great many suppliers. Every contract those suppliers sign ends up, sooner or later, with a cyber security team that is short of people and long on clauses. Each clause must be accepted, rejected or escalated. Multiply that by hundreds of contracts and the arithmetic turns unkind.

The usual remedies are hiring, which is slow, or skimming, which is dangerous. 

A third is to give the reviewers a capable first reader. 

That is what Contract Risk Radar does. It checks each clause against the 133 obligations in the policy and proposes one of five verdicts: accept, modify, replace, reject or escalate. Crucially, it shows its working. Each verdict comes with a reason, the contract clause it read and the policy clause it relied on, so reviewers audit an argument rather than build one from scratch.

Machines that are confidently wrong are a familiar hazard. This one is built to know its limits: when unsure, it escalates, and says why.

Confidentiality meant it was measured on synthetic contracts made to resemble the real thing. It now reads the real thing.

Buyers of such tools tend to ask how accurate they are. The better question is what they do when they do not know.

Your next competitive advantage might not be hiring more people.

It might be building an AI workforce. 🤖

Imagine starting your Monday morning.

📩 Your AI assistant summarizes important emails.

📊 Your AI analyst prepares your sales report.

🎯 Your AI sales assistant researches potential customers.

📄 Your AI document assistant extracts key information from contracts and reports.

⚙️ Your AI operations assistant identifies repetitive tasks that could be automated.

Sounds futuristic?

Many of these workflows are already possible with today's AI tools.

But here's what business leaders need to understand:

An AI workforce isn't about replacing every employee. It's about helping your existing team do more valuable work.

Here's how I'd approach it:

1. Find the bottleneck.
Identify the repetitive task consuming the most time.

2. Calculate the cost.
Measure the hours spent, the errors made, and the delays caused.

3. Choose the right solution.
A simple automation may be enough. Not every problem needs an AI agent.

4. Keep humans in control.
Add human review wherever accuracy, customer trust, or important decisions matter.

5. Measure the results.

Track time saved, quality, cost, and business impact before scaling.

The biggest mistake?

Buying AI tools before understanding the problem.

The smartest businesses won't be those using the most AI.

They'll be the ones using AI to solve the right problems.

If you could build one AI employee for your business today, what job would you give it?
Sales? Marketing? Finance? Operations? Data analysis?

Stop pausing your search for companies that put you on hold

A recruiter tells you that you are the top finalist, but the decision is on hold.

You pause your job search. You check your inbox every hour. You convince yourself an offer is coming once leadership figures things out.

I get why you wait. You put weeks into multiple rounds of interviews. You do not want to start over from scratch.

Treat every pause as a no.

"On hold" is corporate code for cold feet. Companies freeze hiring because bosses hunt for a mythical unicorn. They want one worker who does three jobs for entry pay. They would rather drown their current team than hire a real human.

When a company wants you, they sign you before anyone else can. When they stall, they bet that you have zero other options.

Protect your own timeline:
1. Submit new applications the same day an employer tells you a role is paused.
2. Send one polite note to leave the door open, then write the job off.
3. Keep interviewing with other teams until a written contract is fully signed.

You wouldn’t hire a person who was never interviewed, tested, or checked.

So why are we hiring AI agents that way? 🤔

Most agent leaderboards show one number. It tells you almost nothing about whether an agent will survive your actual work.

At Threadpool, we're building a calibration system for AI agents of any kind: open-source models, Sarvam-powered workflows, or bring-your-own endpoints. Before an agent gets hired for a step, it earns its place through 5 layers:

🔒 L0: Gate. Is it safe? Does it stay in budget, resist prompt injection, and say “I couldn’t verify this” instead of making up a citation? Fail here and it’s never listed.

🧰 L1: Core agentic. Tool use, browsing, multi-step reasoning (GAIA, τ-bench, BrowseComp).

🎯 L2: Capability. Tested only on what it claims to do. 167 capabilities, from financial analysis to contract review.

🇮🇳 L3: Indic languages. Hindi, Hinglish, code-mixed text.

🧪 L4: Private golden set. Sealed tasks with planted traps, so scores can’t be gamed by memorized public data.

Not every skill has a benchmark, so we're honest about it:

✅ Public (120): a recognized benchmark exists
🟡 Proxy (34): only adjacent ones exist, so we add private tests
🛠️ Custom (13): nothing exists (SEO, pricing, due diligence), so we build it

Three rules we hold ourselves to:

- Success means pass^4: the task must work 4 times in a row, not once
- Every score ships with a 95% confidence interval, because “100% on 1 run” is noise
- The reviewer is never the worker

The result: when you hire an agent for a step, you know what it was actually tested on.

The AI hiring tool is ready to ship, and nobody in the room is certain whose signature it needed.

Legal reviewed the contract. Security reviewed the vendor. The board saw a product update. Each assumed the oversight sat somewhere else.

This is where the distinction in Domain 1 does real work. Corporate governance is the system of practices that directs and controls a company, focused on stakeholder interests and accountability. AI governance is the set of frameworks, policies and processes guiding how AI is developed and deployed, so that it aligns with ethical standards, legal requirements and societal values.

They overlap. They are not substitutes. A company relying on corporate governance alone may never look inside the hiring algorithm, and the bias in it surfaces later as discriminatory practice, legal exposure and lost trust.

The gap is specialised oversight: diverse stakeholder input, regular audits of the system, explicit ownership of bias, transparency and accountability as standing questions rather than incident response.

So the useful exam question, and the useful meeting question, is the same one. Who owns this, and does the existing governance structure actually reach it?

The most overlooked bottleneck in Agentic AI right now is not the agent's reasoning capability, but its ability to reliably hand off context to another agent without data leakage or semantic drift. I have been building multi-agent systems for the last 18 months, and the single biggest failure mode is not a hallucination inside one agent, but a corrupted handshake between two.

Three non-obvious technical constraints that define whether a multi-agent system scales or collapses.

First, the protocol layer is not about communication, it is about contract enforcement. If Agent A delegates a task to Agent B, the handoff must include not just the input and output schema, but also a service-level agreement: timeout, retry budget, acceptable failure modes, and a deterministic rollback path. Teams that treat inter-agent calls as unstructured messages will watch their systems degrade into chaos. The winning architecture treats every agent-to-agent interaction as a verifiable handshake with documented terms.

Second, grounding across agent boundaries is the hardest unsolved problem in production. When Agent A passes a result to Agent B, the context must be verifiable against a shared source of truth. If the first agent hallucinates or truncates data, the second agent cannot detect the error without an independent validation step. I am embedding a "grounding checkpoint" at every handoff: a lightweight verification against the original data source or a deterministic rule set. This adds latency, but it eliminates the cascade of garbage that propagates through ungrounded pipelines.

Third, the economics of multi-agent orchestration are brutal. Every inter-agent call incurs inference cost, latency, and reliability risk. The optimal number of agents is not one, and it is not many. It is the minimum number that can complete the task within the cost and time budget. Teams that over-decompose into too many agents are seeing exponential cost growth with linear accuracy gains. The best pattern is to start with a single agent and only split when the bottleneck is clearly identified.

For hiring managers: I am looking for a role where I can design these protocol-grounded, cost-aware multi-agent systems from scratch. If you are building the next generation of autonomous workflows and need someone who understands inter-agent contract design, grounding strategies, and orchestration economics, I want to talk.

What is the most creative grounding pattern you have seen for ensuring data integrity across agent handoffs?

We recruit across schools, MSPs, the IT channel, EdTech and wider technology teams. Each one is telling us something different about hiring right now.

Schools and trusts: IT roles cover devices, safeguarding, cyber and multiple sites, so the right people are hard to find. The trusts that hire well lead with purpose, variety and the school calendar, not a list of every system they own.

MSPs: good engineers rarely leave over pay. They leave over constant firefighting, certifications that never get booked and no clear next step. Hiring to a contract adds pressure, because the salary is fixed before the role is advertised.

IT resellers: more are asking for account managers who understand service delivery, because so much of their revenue is now recurring.

EdTech and SaaS: founders are weighing a strong seller from outside education against one who already knows how schools buy. If pipeline is needed this academic year, sector knowledge usually wins.

Technology teams: AI is changing what teams look like more than how big they are. Data, security and business systems skills are moving up the list.

Each of these affects the others. A trust's IT decision becomes a reseller conversation, then an MSP deployment, then a renewal for the EdTech vendor on top. Every one of those organisations needs the right people to deliver it.

Our director Ravi Patel has written about each of these this month. Follow him for the detail.

Salesforce's October 19 announcement of a one billion dollar, five-year investment in Spain reads like routine regional expansion, until you reach the hiring model: graduates from across the 90-plus countries in its EMEA South region spend a year training in Madrid alongside Forward Deployed Engineers, then return home to run agentic AI implementations locally.

The detail most AI agent rollouts get wrong is who holds the knowledge once the project ends. If the only people who understand an agent's failure modes are the vendor's own team, that understanding leaves when the contract does. Training people and then physically sending them back into the client's own market keeps it in the building.

We run a narrower version of the same handover: an agent doesn't go live for a client until someone on their side has sat through enough failed tool calls, in person, to debug the next one without us.

Navigating the Invisible Gatekeepers: Generation Z and the Contemporary Labor Market

In the shifting landscape of work, Generation Z has emerged as a cohort whose entry into professional life reveals profound transformations in economic structures, cultural expectations, and organizational practices. Born roughly between the mid-1990s and early 2010s, this generation confronts a labor market marked by algorithmic intermediaries, diminished entry-level pathways, and a pervasive sense of precarity.

From business anthropology’s standpoint, these challenges are not merely economic statistics, but lived cultural experiences that reshape rituals of job seeking, redefine notions of value and competence, and alter the social contracts between individuals and institutions. Anthony Galima states: “Business anthropology draws on ethnographic insight to examine how people make meaning within organizational and market systems. It attends to symbols, practices, power dynamics, and the informal rules that govern economic life. Applied to Generation Z’s job market struggles, this lens illuminates how traditional pathways to adulthood and economic independence have fractured.”

Earlier generations often moved from education into relatively predictable employment hierarchies. High School led to blue collar jobs while college led to specialized fields. All you needed was a resume and handshake. 

Today’s young adults encounter systems that prioritize efficiency and risk minimization over human development. Central to this experience is the rise of automated screening technologies. Applicant tracking systems and AI-driven filters now process the majority of resumes before any human recruiter reviews them. Estimates suggest that around 75 percent of applications never reach a person. For Generation Z, this creates a ritual of mass submission: hundreds or even thousands of applications dispatched into digital voids, followed by prolonged silence or automated rejections.

Anthropologically, this resembles a high-stakes, low-feedback initiation rite in which the candidate performs competence according to opaque algorithmic criteria rather than demonstrated potential or cultural fit. The process strips away relational elements that once characterized hiring, such as informal referrals or face-to-face impressions, and replaces them with quantifiable signals that favor those already possessing conventional markers of experience.

Entry-level opportunities themselves have contracted. Employers increasingly list roles requiring years of prior experience for positions once considered starting points.  #BusinessAnthropology #AI #JobSeekers
